Myth. "My customers will call back if I miss them."

Most won't. They call the next business on the list, and that one gets the job.

A missed call isn't a delay. It's usually a lost sale.

Five minute fix for today.

Set up an automatic text that goes out the moment you miss a call.

"Sorry I missed you, I'm on a job. What can I help with?"

Most phones and business lines can do this. It keeps the customer talking to you instead of dialing someone else.

James Clear says it plainly in Atomic Habits. You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.

A goal of more customers means nothing if nobody answers the phone at 6 PM.

Build the system and the goal takes care of itself.

Quick one for owners.

What time of day do you miss the most calls?

A) Early morning
B) Midday on a job
C) After 5 PM
D) Weekends

Reply with your letter. That's where your money is leaking.

Build note from this week.

My Threads posts went quiet for two days. The script that posts them did exactly what I designed it to do. It found nothing approved, failed loudly, and emailed me.

The bug wasn't in the code. Nobody owned writing the next week.

Every automation needs an owner. Who owns yours?

Your competitor isn't better than you.

They just picked up the phone.

Here's what I build, straight.

AI that answers every call, texts back every missed one, follows up on every quote, and asks every happy customer for a Google review.

$997 to set up, then $297 a month, month to month. The first 3 founding clients pay $497 setup in exchange for a testimonial.

DM me MONEY if you want one of the 3.

Answer the phone today like rent depends on it.

Because it does.

Today is Veterans Day.

To every veteran who served and then went on to build a business, thank you. Discipline, systems, and showing up when it's hard are the same skills that keep a business alive.

Follow up script you can steal today.

"Hi [name], just checking in on the quote I sent for [job]. Happy to answer any questions or adjust anything. Want me to hold a spot on the schedule for you?"

Short, friendly, and it asks for the next step. Send it to every quote that went quiet this month.

Alex Hormozi breaks value into four parts in $100M Offers.

The result they want, how sure they are they'll get it, how long it takes, and how much effort it costs them.

You don't always need a lower price. Make it faster, easier, and more certain, and the same price suddenly looks cheap.

Honest question.

How many days do you wait before following up on a quote?

A) Same day
B) 2 to 3 days
C) A week
D) I don't follow up

No judgment. Reply with your letter and I'll tell you what I'd change.

Use AI to write your follow ups once and reuse them forever.

1. Tell ChatGPT or Claude what you sell and who buys it.
2. Ask for a follow up text for day 1, day 3, and day 7 after a quote.
3. Save them as text shortcuts on your phone.

Now following up takes 10 seconds, so you'll actually do it.

Most deals aren't lost to a cheaper competitor.

They're lost to silence.

Free thing for home service pros.

My 5 Star Review Kit has 7 copy and paste messages that get happy customers to leave Google reviews, plus a timing cheat sheet so you know what to send and when.

Grab it at evogencyglobal.com/free-review-kit

No catch. Use it this week and tell me how many reviews it brings in.
The follow up you didn't send today is the job someone else books tomorrow.

Here's who works for me.

One bot finds real estate listings worth pitching. One builds a demo page for each. One drafts the outreach. One writes content. One runs my morning brief.

They do the legwork. I check the work and make the calls.

What's the first job you'd hand to a bot?

Steal this Google review routine.

1. Finish the job.
2. Within 2 hours, text the customer a thank you with your review link.
3. If they haven't left one in 3 days, send one friendly reminder.

Timing matters more than wording. Ask while they're still happy.

Michael Gerber made this point famous, and it still hits.

Most small business owners work in their business all day and never work on it.

Block one hour this week to work on it. Fix one process, write one script, or automate one task you repeat every day.

Owners, be honest.

If you took a week off, what would break first?

A) The phones
B) Scheduling
C) Quotes and follow ups
D) Everything

Reply with your letter. That's the first system to build.

One prompt that saves you an hour a week.

"Here are the 10 questions customers ask me most [paste them]. Write a short, friendly answer to each that I can text or email. Keep each under 3 sentences."

Save the answers. Stop typing the same thing every day.

Reviews are the cheapest salesperson you'll ever hire.

They work 24 hours a day and never ask for a raise. All you have to do is ask for them.

Two ways to work with me.

We run it. I set up your AI front desk and run it for $297 a month, month to month, no contract.

You own it. You pay once, I build it in your own accounts and hand you the keys.

Either way, every call gets answered. DM me MONEY and tell me which fits.

Work on your business tonight for 15 minutes.

Your future self will thank you.

Unpopular opinion. Nobody reads your website before they call.

They read your reviews, look at your photos, and call whoever looks trustworthy.

Your reviews are your sales pitch.

Prompt Friday. Turn one job into a week of content.

"I just finished [describe the job]. Write 3 short social posts about it. One about the problem, one about how we fixed it, and one tip the customer can use. Keep each under 60 words."

One job, three posts, zero blank page.

Daniel Pink's argument in To Sell Is Human is that everyone is in sales now.

If you answer the phone, write a quote, or explain a price, you're selling.

Stop thinking of selling as pushy. Think of it as helping someone make a decision they already want to make.

Friday question.

What's one task you do every week that you hate doing by hand?

Tell me below. I'll reply with how I'd automate it.

Second prompt for your Friday. This one finds your best customers.

"Here's a list of my jobs from the last 3 months with the price of each [paste it]. Which type of customer and job makes me the most money for the least time? What should I do more of?"

You might be busy with the wrong work.

Busy feels productive.

Profitable is what pays the bills. Know the difference.

Plain offer for the weekend.

I'm taking 3 founding clients for my AI front desk. You get setup for $497 instead of $997, and I get an honest testimonial and a case study.

It answers every call, books the job, and texts back anyone you miss.

DM me MONEY to claim a spot.

Somebody needs a plumber, an electrician, or a roofer tonight.

The business that answers wins.

Saturday reminder. Your customers don't take weekends off from having problems.

If your phone goes to voicemail all weekend, so does your revenue.

Saturday money check, 10 minutes.

1. Count the calls you missed this week.
2. Count the quotes you sent that never got a follow up.
3. Count the finished jobs that never got a review request.

Those three numbers are your to do list for Monday.

Robert Cialdini calls it social proof in Influence. When people aren't sure, they look at what others did.

That's why a business with 200 reviews gets the call over one with 12, even when the work is the same.

Ask every happy customer for a review. Every single one.

Weekend question for builders.

What's the best business decision you made this year?

Drop it below. Someone reading needs to hear it.

What I'm proud of this week.

The posts you're reading are written with AI, checked by me, and published by a script I wrote that posts every 2 hours on the minute.

When it broke, it told me exactly why within minutes. That's the part I designed on purpose.

Build systems that fail loudly, not quietly.

People don't remember your price.

They remember how fast you showed up and whether you did what you said.

If your business runs on the phone, I'll do one thing for you free.

DM me MONEY and I'll work out what your missed calls are probably costing you, using your own numbers.

No pitch unless you ask for one.

Rest tonight.

The systems you built this week can keep working without you.

Sunday truth. Revenue is vanity if none of it is left at the end of the month.

Know your numbers before you chase more sales.

Sunday planning, 15 minutes.

1. Write down the 3 things that would make the most money this week.
2. Put them on your calendar before anything else.
3. Ask AI to draft the emails or texts each one needs.

Walk into Monday with a plan instead of an inbox.

Mike Michalowicz flips the formula in Profit First.

Most owners pay every bill and keep whatever is left. He says take your profit first and run the business on the rest.

Even 1% set aside every time you get paid builds the habit.

Owners, honest Sunday question.

What's one thing you'll do differently this week?

Answer faster, follow up more, raise a price, or ask for reviews? Pick one and tell me below.

Weekly review prompt for Sunday night.

"Here's what I did in my business this week [paste a quick list]. What worked, what wasted my time, and what's the one thing I should focus on next week?"

Ten minutes with AI beats a week of guessing.

Speed sells.

First to answer, first to quote, first to follow up. That's how small businesses beat big ones.

The offer for the week ahead.

I build AI that answers your calls, books your jobs, follows up on your quotes, and asks for your reviews. I run it for you, or I build it in your accounts so you own it.

3 founding spots at $497 setup.

DM me MONEY to grab one, or get my free review kit at evogencyglobal.com/free-review-kit

New week tomorrow.

Answer every call. Follow up every quote. Ask for every review.
